transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

I keep getting these flashes out of nowhere. I’ll be standing at a pickup counter and suddenly it’s like I’m back in that crowded holding room, seeing the fight and hearing everyone getting shoved against the wall.
Did that event involve a time when you thought you might be seriously hurt or killed?
I’m not sure. It was chaotic, and I remember being scared, but I don’t know if I thought I was going to be killed.
During that incident, did you think you might die or be seriously injured?
I—I don’t really know. I was scared and it felt out of control, but I can’t say I was thinking, “I’m going to die,” or that I knew I’d be seriously hurt.
When these flashes happen, do you suddenly feel a wave of intense panic?
I’m not sure I’d call it panic. It’s more like I get startled and thrown off for a moment.
During that incident, were you physically hurt or directly threatened with serious harm?
I don’t think I was physically hurt. As for being directly threatened… I can’t really say for sure. It all happened so fast.
When these flashes happen, do you feel detached from yourself or from what’s around you?
I’m not sure. I don’t think I feel detached exactly—I just get kind of thrown off for a moment.
When these flashes happen, does it feel like you are actually back in that room and reliving it in the moment?

Yeah… sometimes it does. I’ll be standing at a pickup counter and all of a sudden it’s like I’m back in that crowded holding room, seeing the fight and hearing everyone getting shoved against the wall.
How long have these flashbacks been happening?
About a week now—since I was detained overnight and saw that assault in the holding area.
Since that night, have you been avoiding places or situations that remind you of what happened?

Yeah. I’ve been turning down night runs and taking the long way around town so I don’t have to go near that detention building. And talking about it—I can’t really do that without feeling like I’m right back there.
Have these symptoms lasted longer than one month?
No, it’s only been about a week—since that night I was detained and saw what happened.
During that assault in the holding area, did you believe your life or someone else’s life was in danger?
I’m not sure. It all happened so fast—I just remember being scared and trying to stay out of it.
Did it seem to you that the person being assaulted might be killed or seriously injured?
I don’t know. I saw it happening, but I couldn’t tell how bad it was going to get. I just remember being scared and trying not to get involved.
When you saw the assault, did it seem to you that the person was in immediate danger of being seriously injured?
I honestly couldn’t tell in that moment. It was chaotic, and I was scared, but I didn’t know whether he was seriously hurt right then.
Since that night, have you felt emotionally numb?
I’m not really sure what you mean by numb. I’ve been scared, but I don’t know if I’d call it numb.
Since that night, have you been jumpier than usual, like getting easily startled by sudden noises or movements?

Yeah. Every radio crackle, siren, or even a door slamming makes me jump like someone’s about to rush me. Then my heart pounds so hard afterward I sometimes have to pull over or step outside for a minute.
Since that night, have there been moments when things around you felt unreal or dreamlike?
I don’t think so. Things have felt stressful, but I haven’t really noticed them seeming unreal or dreamlike.
Since that night, have you been unable to remember an important part of what happened in the holding area?

Yeah. I remember bits—the guy on the floor, the officers yelling—but how the fight actually started is just missing. It’s like my mind skips over those few minutes no matter how hard I try to remember.
Since that night, have you been having nightmares about what happened?
Yeah. I barely sleep now. I’ll doze off for an hour or two, then wake up from a dream about that cell, or a door slamming. By morning I’m so wrecked I don’t feel like I can drive my route.
Since that night, have these symptoms made it hard for you to do your usual work or daily activities?

Yeah, a lot. I’ve already missed two shifts. When I try to work, I don’t feel safe driving or handling deliveries—I’m too shaken and on edge. And I stopped going to my volunteer commitments too. I just can’t keep it together around people right now.
When you saw the assault in the holding area, did you believe the person being attacked might die?
I’m not sure. Everything happened so fast, and I can’t really remember enough of it to say what I believed at the time.
